extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific reasoning, logic, and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and distinguish the main forms of inference used in science (deduction, induction, hypothesis), their relations, strengths, and proper methods for producing and testing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction (syllogistic/Barbara form)
rubrics_metrics.description: All deduction is the application of general rules to particular cases; syllogisms like Barbara (S is M; M is P; therefore S is P) exemplify deductive reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deduction lays down a major premise (a rule), states a minor premise (a case under the rule), and draws the conclusion by applying the rule to the case. Deductive inference adds nothing beyond the premises — it merely selects and brings attention to a fact represented there. Examples: classical syllogisms (Barbara); probabilistic deductions (when a rule about proportions plus a sampling procedure yields a probability for the drawn item).

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction (synthetic inference/generalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction infers a rule from observed cases and results — generalizing from particulars to a general law or to the same proportion in the whole class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induction is where we generalize from a number of cases of which something is true and infer it true of a whole class, or infer proportions for the whole from sample proportions. It is the inference of a rule from case and result (inversion of a deductive syllogism). Inductions can be very strong but are weakened when stretched beyond observed limits and require explanatory support when extrapolated. Empirical formulae derived by induction are useful descriptions but are not of the highest scientific rank unless they become laws that contain no unnecessary arbitrary constants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (inference of a case from rule and result / explanation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis infers the existence of an unobserved case or cause from a rule and an observed result; often supposes something different from what has been directly observed and is generally weaker than induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothesis is the inference of a case from a rule and result (or of a cause from an effect) and is often a bolder and more perilous step than induction. Typical uses: inferring authorship from a matching torn paper edge; explaining fossils by supposing the sea once covered the land; inferring historic persons from documents. Hypotheses frequently propose facts not directly observable and so may not be replaceable by induction but rather supported by a variety of consequences and connections to other laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification scheme for inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: All inferences can be classified as Deductive (analytic) or Synthetic; synthetic inferences further divide into Induction and Hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deduction = application of general rules to particular cases. Synthetic splits into Induction (generalizing from similar observed cases to unobserved similar cases) and Hypothesis (inferring causes or unobserved facts of a different kind from observed effects). This classification is useful for analyzing the character, strength, and appropriate methods of different scientific inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect moods (Baroco and Bocardo) and their probabilistic counterparts
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain syllogistic moods (Baroco and Bocardo) are 'indirect' moods that deny a result and thereby deny either the case or the rule; when applied probabilistically they correspond to hypothesis and induction respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: From a probable Barbara-type premise, denying the result while accepting the rule yields a denial of the case (hypothetic inference); denying the result while accepting the case yields a denial of the rule (inductive inference). Indirect moods require transformations to appear as applications of a rule to a case and illuminate relations between denial of conclusions and what must be denied among premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for making a hypothesis probable
rubrics_metrics.description: To make hypothesis formation lead to probable results, follow specific procedural safeguards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three explicit rules given: (1) The hypothesis should be distinctly put as a question before making the observations intended to test it (i.e., use predictions from the hypothesis). (2) The respects in which resemblances are noted must be taken at random — do not cherry-pick kinds of predictions for which the hypothesis is known to be good. (3) Failures as well as successes of predictions must be honestly noted; the whole proceeding must be fair and unbiased. These rules guard against confirmatory bias and partisan methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inferring wider similarity from isolated resemblances
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong resemblance in some respects between two things does not justify inferring similarity in other respects without further reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on selective or recondite resemblances (e.g., comparative mythologists finding many resemblances and inferring identity of meaning). Resemblances must be considered fairly and not picked to fit a favored hypothesis; otherwise the inference is weak or fallacious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses should be connected to known laws and explain deviations
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis gains strength when it explains an empirical formula/law and also accounts for deviations from that formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful theories are not pure guesses but are guided by reasons and connections to established principles (e.g., kinetical theory of gases explaining Boyle's law and small deviations when linked with mechanical theory of heat). A hypothesis supported by other laws or by multiple kinds of observed facts becomes more credible and may develop into a theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between empirical formulae and laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical formulae are inductive descriptions of observations; laws of nature are formulae that contain no more arbitrary numbers than required by measurement scales and can serve as bases for hypotheses/theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical formulae (e.g., polynomial fits) are useful descriptive tools but may not be exact due to observational errors and formula error. When a formula exhibits invariance beyond measurement conventions and is explainable by reasons, it attains the status of a law and is often the object of hypothetical explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrapolation weakens inductive warrant unless explanatory support exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive inferences become weaker the further they extend beyond observed experience; substantial extrapolation requires explanatory reasons to be credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no sharp line where induction ceases to warrant belief, but the farther an induction is pushed beyond observed limits the weaker it becomes. To justify wide extrapolation one should find that the extension explains some observed facts; most physical theories involve a mixture of induction and hypothesis that support one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological/physiological modes corresponding to inference types
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction, hypothesis, and deduction correspond to different psychological/physiological processes: induction forms habit, hypothesis produces a sensuous/emotional element, and deduction corresponds to attention/volition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is descriptive guidance for understanding how different inferences are apprehended: induction expresses formation of a habit (rule-belief), hypothesis bundles many predicates into a single intense conception producing an 'emotion' akin to aesthetic or sensuous satisfaction, and deduction selects and focuses upon particular facts represented in premises. Awareness of these modes can help diagnose cognitive biases and the experiential difference between types of reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness and disinterestedness as methodological requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific reasoning requires a real desire to know the truth; methods of obstinacy, authority, partisan debate, and trying to reach a foregone conclusion are of no value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logic demonstrates that knowledge advances by honest inquiry; investigators must avoid partisan tactics and biased argumentation. The investigator must ask 'Do I want to know how the fact stands?' and proceed only if genuinely seeking truth.
